newsitem.title: USA: Jobs, higher prices cited in China trade decision.
newsitem.headline: Jobs, higher prices cited in China trade decision.

text.p: Higher U.S. prices for imports, loss of jobs and a possible disruption of Hong Kong's economic stability helped shape Washington's decision to renew favoured trading status for China, officials said on Monday.

Revocation of the status "would cost U.S. consumers almost $600 million annually for goods such as shoes, clothing and small appliances," U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky told a briefing after President Bill Clinton announced that he planned to renew the trading status.

"U.S. exports to China have more than trebled (tripled) over the past decade," she added. "Those exports support more than 170,000 U.S. jobs." She said revocation could trigger retaliation against U.S. exports and open the China market to competitors.

Barshefsky said Hong Kong "is the gateway of trade between the United States and China and handles more than 50 percent of U.S.-Chinese trade. Undercutting the island's economic footing at this moment would be a serious blow, just at the time when Hong Kong needs to assert its strength ..."
She added that Hong Kong officials have estimated revocation would slash its U.S. trade by between 20 and 30 percent, resulting in a loss of as many as 85,000 jobs there.
National Security Adviser Sandy Berger told the same briefing that the United States "must support the economic vitality of Hong Kong during the transition" to Chinese rule this summer.

He said the White House would probably notify Congress formally of its intention to renew the trading status shortly and said it would be up to the congressional leadership to set the timetable for the debate over efforts to disapprove of the decision.
"We would hope to be able to sustain the president's decision in the process," he said.
To block Clinton's decision, Congress would have to vote it down and then have to muster a two-thirds vote to overturn a likely Clinton veto.
